lesson.title: Sense the Sugar: Induction and the Lac Operon
lesson.summary: The lac operon is an inducible operon that stays off by default and switches on only when lactose is present, with a second layer of control that boosts transcription further when glucose, the cell's preferred sugar, is scarce.
lesson.body:
The lac operon in the bacterium Escherichia coli contains three structural genes, lacZ, lacY, and lacA, transcribed together as one mRNA under a single promoter. LacZ encodes the enzyme beta-galactosidase, which breaks lactose down into glucose and galactose. LacY encodes lactose permease, a membrane transport protein that brings lactose into the cell in the first place. Together, these genes let a cell that has them switched on take up and digest the sugar lactose. The operon is a clear example of negative control layered with positive control, and of an inducible system: one that is normally off and is switched on by the presence of a specific molecule.

A separate gene, lacI, is expressed continuously at a low, steady level and produces the Lac repressor protein. When lactose is absent from the cell, the Lac repressor binds directly to the operator, a DNA sequence overlapping the lac promoter, and that binding physically blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon. In this default state, with no lactose around, the lac operon is off, and the cell makes almost none of the enzymes needed to digest a sugar it does not have.

When lactose is available, a small amount of it is converted inside the cell into allolactose, an isomer of lactose that serves as the actual inducer molecule. Allolactose binds to the Lac repressor and changes its shape so that it can no longer bind the operator. With the repressor released, RNA polymerase is free to transcribe lacZYA. This is why the operon is called inducible: lactose, indirectly through allolactose, induces its own breakdown by releasing the block on transcription.

Removing the repressor is not, by itself, enough for strong transcription, because the lac promoter is intrinsically weak. A second regulatory protein, the catabolite activator protein, or CAP, provides positive control. CAP only binds DNA effectively when it is itself bound to a small molecule called cyclic AMP, or cAMP, and cellular cAMP levels rise specifically when glucose is scarce. When CAP is bound to cAMP, it attaches to a site next to the lac promoter and helps RNA polymerase bind there far more efficiently, sharply increasing transcription.

Putting both controls together produces four possible situations. With no lactose present, the repressor stays bound to the operator regardless of glucose, and the operon stays off. With lactose present and glucose also present, the repressor is released, but cAMP levels are low, so CAP is inactive and transcription stays low. With lactose present and glucose absent, the repressor is released and CAP, now bound to cAMP, is fully active, so transcription is strong, and the operon is fully on. And with glucose present but no lactose, the operon is off for the same reason as the first case: the repressor is bound. In practice this means the lac operon reaches its highest activity only when lactose is available and glucose is not, which is exactly the condition under which the cell actually benefits from breaking lactose down: glucose, its preferred and more easily used energy source, is the first sugar a cell exhausts when both are offered together, and lac operon activity then rises to let the cell switch over to using lactose instead.
